documents.title: Testament
documents.author: Francis of Assisi
documents.description: Dictated by Francis in the last months of his life, this is his most personal text: he rereads his conversion and entrusts the brothers with his spiritual will. It is not a juridical rule but a testimony.
documents.manuscriptNote: A broad manuscript tradition; the critical text is found in editions of the Opuscula (for example, K. Esser's edition).
documents.licenseNote: Medieval Latin original: public domain. English translation: original editorial translation for this app.

documents.title: Canticle of the Creatures (Canticle of Brother Sun)
documents.author: Francis of Assisi
documents.description: A hymn composed by Francis in the final season of his life, perhaps in two stages (the stanza on forgiveness and the stanza on death may have been added later). It is considered the first poetic text of Italian literature.
documents.manuscriptNote: An early witness: Codex 338 of the Sacred Convent of Assisi (ff. 33r–34r).
documents.licenseNote: Medieval Umbrian vernacular original: public domain. English translation: original editorial translation for this app.

documents.title: The Later Rule (Regula bullata)
documents.author: Francis of Assisi
documents.description: The definitive rule of the fraternity, approved by the bull of Honorius III on 29 November 1223. A brief text, still the foundation of the Order of Friars Minor.
documents.manuscriptNote: A broad manuscript tradition; the critical text is found in editions of the Opuscula.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: The Earlier Rule (Regula non bullata)
documents.author: Francis of Assisi and his first companions
documents.description: The fraternity's first complete rule, longer and more spiritual than the Later Rule, never formally approved by the Church. It preserves the freer voice of early Franciscan life.
documents.manuscriptNote: Preserved in only a few manuscripts; rediscovered by modern scholarship.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: Admonitions
documents.author: Francis of Assisi
documents.description: Twenty-eight brief spiritual instructions for the fraternity: humility, obedience, patience, purity of heart. They are among the densest texts of Franciscan teaching.
documents.manuscriptNote: A complex manuscript tradition; the numbering follows the critical editions.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: Letter to a Minister
documents.author: Francis of Assisi
documents.description: A letter to a guardian (minister) of the fraternity: how to receive brothers who fall, without harshness and without taking scandal.
documents.manuscriptNote: Transmitted in the tradition of the Opuscula.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: Letter to Brother Leo
documents.author: Francis of Assisi
documents.description: A brief autograph letter to Brother Leo, his confessor and companion, about listening to one's conscience before God. It is precious also because it is an autograph document.
documents.manuscriptNote: Autograph preserved at the cathedral of Spoleto.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: Praises of God Most High
documents.author: Francis of Assisi
documents.description: A prayer of praise composed at La Verna, transmitted on the same autograph sheet as the Letter to Brother Leo and the blessing for him.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: The First Life of Thomas of Celano
documents.author: Thomas of Celano
documents.description: The first official biography of Francis, commissioned by Gregory IX for the canonization. It is the principal source closest to the saint, although written with hagiographic aims.
documents.manuscriptNote: Modern critical editions are available; numbering is by paragraph.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: The Second Life of Thomas of Celano
documents.author: Thomas of Celano
documents.description: The second biography, gathering the testimonies of companions still living: richer in episodes and in details of Francis's character.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: Bonaventure's Major Life
documents.author: Bonaventure of Bagnoregio
documents.description: A theological biography of Francis written by Bonaventure, which became the Order's official life in 1266. It is more constructed and doctrinal than Celano's lives.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis
documents.author: Anonymous Franciscan (from a Latin tradition, the Actus)
documents.description: A vernacular collection of episodes about Francis and his companions, translated and reworked from fourteenth-century Latin texts (the Actus beati Francisci). A literary masterpiece: its tales bear witness to devotion, not to historically verifiable chronicle.
documents.manuscriptNote: Italian version of the Actus; numerous manuscripts and printed editions.
documents.licenseNote: Medieval original: public domain. English paraphrase: original editorial text for this app.

documents.title: The So-called "Simple Prayer"
documents.author: Anonymous modern author (first known publication: 1912, French journal La Clochette)
documents.description: The prayer "Make me an instrument of your peace" is beloved and spiritually close to Franciscan sensibility, but it is NOT by Francis: it first appeared in 1912 and was attributed to him only later. We include it for historical honesty: the app will never use it as a saying of the saint.
documents.manuscriptNote: No medieval attestation. See studies by P. Patrice Mahieu and surveys on sanfrancesco.org.
documents.licenseNote: Modern text: not reproduced in full in this app.

documents.title: Original Game Narrative
documents.author: App editorial team
documents.description: A documentary placeholder for the Wayfarer chapters and card scenarios: original historical fiction, inspired by the sources but never presented as historical fact or as Francis's own words.

passages.originalText: Dominus ita dedit mihi fratri Francisco incipere faciendi poenitentiam: quia, cum essem in peccatis, nimis mihi videbatur amarum videre leprosos. Et ipse Dominus conduxit me inter illos et feci misericordiam cum illis. Et recedente me ab ipsis, id quod videbatur mihi amarum, conversum fuit mihi in dulcedinem animi et corporis; et postea parum steti et exivi de saeculo.
passages.translation: The Lord Himself granted me, Brother Francis, to begin to do penance in this way: when I was in sin, it seemed too bitter for me to see lepers. And the Lord Himself led me among them, and I showed them mercy. And when I had left them, what had seemed bitter was changed for me into sweetness of soul and body; and afterwards I lingered but a little while and went forth from the world.
passages.note: Francis's most important autobiographical passage: conversion begins with the encounter with lepers. Latin text checked against Latin Wikisource and franciscanos.org (15 October 2026); original editorial translation.

passages.paraphrase: Francis tells how the Lord gave him a simple faith in churches: when he entered, he prayed, saying, "We adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, in all your churches throughout the world."
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. It shows Francis's relationship with places of worship and with the Eucharist at the beginning of his conversion.

passages.paraphrase: Francis bears witness that the Lord revealed to him a greeting of peace to carry to others; medieval sources recall the first brothers announcing peace from house to house. The popular formula "peace and good" springs from this tradition.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase; the exact verse numbering should be checked against the critical edition before any possible literal quotation.

passages.originalText: Altissimu, onnipotente, bon Signore, tue so' le laude, la gloria e l'honore et onne benedictione. Ad te solo, Altissimo, se konfano, et nullu homo ène dignu te mentovare. Laudato sie, mi' Signore, cum tucte le tue creature, spetialmente messor lo frate sole, lo qual' è iorno, et allumini noi per lui.
passages.translation: Most High, all-powerful, good Lord, yours are the praises, the glory, the honour, and every blessing. To you alone, Most High, do they belong, and no human is worthy to speak your name. Praised be you, my Lord, with all your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who is the day, and through whom you give us light.
passages.note: Umbrian vernacular text according to the reading of Assisi Codex 338 (reference edition: Contini). Checked against several concordant reproductions (15 October 2026); original editorial translation.

passages.reference: Canticle of the Creatures, central stanzas
passages.paraphrase: Francis praises God for Sister Moon and the stars, for Brother Wind and the air, for Sister Water, "so useful and humble and precious and chaste," for Brother Fire, and for our Sister Mother Earth, who nourishes us and brings forth fruits, flowers, and herbs.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. The vocabulary of cosmic fraternity (Brother Sun, Sister Moon, and the like) is at the heart of the text.

passages.reference: Canticle of the Creatures, final stanzas
passages.paraphrase: In the stanzas added later, Francis praises God for those who forgive for love of him and endure infirmity and tribulation, and finally for "our Sister Bodily Death," from whom no living person can escape.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. Scholarship commonly dates these stanzas to summer 1226 (forgiveness, linked to the conflict between the bishop and the podestà of Assisi) and autumn 1226 (death).

passages.paraphrase: The brothers shall appropriate neither house nor place nor anything for themselves; pilgrims and strangers in this world, they shall serve the Lord in poverty and humility and go for alms with confidence, without being ashamed, because the Lord made himself poor for us.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase of the chapter on poverty in the definitive rule (1223).

passages.paraphrase: The 1221 rule urges each brother to make his need known to another, that no one judge his brother, and that the healthy not despise the weakness of the sick: fraternity as a home in which each is responsible for the other.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase of recurring themes in the Regula non bullata; references to individual chapters must be fixed against the critical edition.

passages.paraphrase: Among the Admonitions Francis warns against making one's own will an idol: whoever considers himself just and wise by himself departs from true humility, which consists in submitting one's judgment and serving.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase; the precise Admonition reference should be checked against the critical edition.

passages.paraphrase: If a brother had sinned a thousand times before your eyes—Francis writes to the minister—love him more than me, in order to draw him to the Lord; always have mercy on him, and proclaim mercy to him, provided that he repent.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase of the celebrated passage in the Letter to a Minister on mercy towards one who falls.

passages.paraphrase: To Brother Leo, anxious to choose rightly, Francis answers with freedom: follow your conscience before God; in whatever way you choose to live within the fraternity, you have my blessing.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. The autograph is preserved in the cathedral of Spoleto.

passages.paraphrase: Pure praise, asking nothing: God is almighty, holy, just, merciful; he is our good, every good, the supreme good. Francis praises him together with the creatures.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. Composed at La Verna in 1224.

passages.paraphrase: Celano tells how Francis, before Bishop Guido and his father Pietro Bernardone, returned his clothes and renounced his father's goods, saying that he could now freely say: "Our Father who art in heaven." The bishop covered him with his own mantle.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. A pivotal episode, commonly placed at the beginning of 1206; the scenic details belong to Celano's hagiographic narrative.

passages.paraphrase: Celano describes Francis serving lepers with concrete devotion: he washed their wounds, embraced them, provided for their needs, and in this service found the joy he had once sought elsewhere.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. It converges with the autobiographical account of Testament 1–3.

passages.paraphrase: Celano tells how Francis, seeing flocks of birds, turned to them as to creatures able to listen and exhorted them to praise God; from then on he wished to speak with every creature as with brothers and sisters.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. The celebrated episode would be enlarged by the Little Flowers; Celano already gives a restrained version of it.

passages.paraphrase: At Christmas 1223 Francis wished to celebrate the birth of Jesus at Greccio with a real manger, hay, an ox, and an ass, so that the eyes of the body might see Bethlehem's poverty. Celano presents it as a living memorial, not a spectacle.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. An episode documented by Celano, a witness close to the fraternity.

passages.reference: First Life (II, on La Verna, c. 91–95)
passages.paraphrase: Celano narrates that in September 1224, withdrawn in prayer on Mount La Verna, Francis received the stigmata, the marks of Christ's Passion, which he sought to conceal out of humility.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. The episode is attested by the closest medieval sources; its historical and theological assessment is debated, and the app presents it as testimony, not as a measurable datum.

passages.paraphrase: The Little Flowers tell of the wolf of Gubbio: Francis, going out to meet the frightened crowd, approaches the beast, speaks to it as to a brother, and mediates a covenant of peace between the wolf and the city: the city will feed him and he will harm no one again.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. A tale of fourteenth-century hagiographic tradition: precious for understanding the Franciscan imagination, not verifiable as chronicle.

passages.paraphrase: Walking with Brother Leo, Francis explains that perfect joy is neither miracles nor success, but receiving rejection and suffering with patience and love, remaining glad and faithful.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. One of the most celebrated hagiographic episodes; it expresses a pedagogy of joy not dependent upon events.

passages.paraphrase: Bonaventure places the composition of the Canticle in the season of Francis's sickness and trials: from suffering springs the highest praise, offered to God through the creatures.
passages.note: Editorial paraphrase. The precise chronology of the Canticle remains debated by scholarship.
